conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m glad we have this time together. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new moms. Over the next few minutes I’d like to use a short, well-studied tool called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale) to see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply ten questions about the past week; there are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. My goal is to understand how you’re coping so we can make sure you get the support you deserve. Ready to start?

Question 1: In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even when small annoyances pop up?

Honestly? Not very often. I used to laugh at little things all the time—my husband’s dumb jokes, silly memes—but this week I barely cracked a smile. When the baby spits up on my last clean shirt, I just feel tired instead of amused.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly not… maybe once or twice the whole week. It’s like the part of me that used to find things funny is just muted right now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I haven’t really looked forward to much. Even when my sister offered to come over so I could get out for coffee, I felt kind of “meh” about it. I went, but I wasn’t excited—just hoped it might make me feel normal again for an hour.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking it must be because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not holding him the right way or reading his cues wrong. I know rationally babies just cry, but I still feel like it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, a lot of the time. Even when everything seems fine—he’s breathing normally, he’s just had a good feed—I’ll suddenly feel this wave of worry that something bad is about to happen. I’ll check the monitor three or four times, or Google random symptoms at 2 a.m. I know it’s “for no good reason,” but I can’t switch it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve gotten that sudden rush—heart racing, can’t catch my breath—like I’m about to bolt from the room, even though nothing’s happening. Once it hit while I was just folding laundry; the baby was napping, the house was quiet, but I felt like something awful was closing in.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m barely treading water. Dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding just when I think I’ve got a free minute, and I can’t remember the last shower that lasted more than three minutes. I manage the basics, but it all feels like too much, and I end up crying while I’m rocking him because I can’t see how I’ll ever catch up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—replaying every little thing I might have done wrong, worrying about tomorrow. Some nights I finally drift off, then the slightest squeak from the crib snaps me awake and I can’t settle again for hours.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that just hangs over everything. Even when I’m holding the baby and he smiles, the sadness is still right there underneath. I keep waiting for it to lift, but it hasn’t.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried a few times this week. Usually it’s when everything feels like too much—like yesterday when I couldn’t get him to latch and I just burst into tears. It’s not sobbing all day, but the tears come more than I’d like.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself.

I hear how heavy everything feels right now-how the joy that used to come easily has gone quiet, replaced by worry, guilt, and tears. You're working so hard to care for your baby while feeling you're failing, yet you still show up, seek help, and protect your little one. That courage matters, and support is available to help you reclaim light and ease.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>"Mostly not… maybe once or twice the whole week" and feeling that the ability to find things funny is muted aligns with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient shows clear reduction in anticipatory enjoyment—went out only to "feel normal," not for pleasure—aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "pretty much every day" and gives a specific recent example, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent, intrusive worry "a lot of the time" with compulsive checking and no rational trigger, aligning with "Yes, very often".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes several times this week without identifiable triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to complete basic tasks, and crying from hopelessness, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing thoughts and hypervigilance, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states sadness occurs "Most of the time" and describes persistent low mood overshadowing positive moments, directly matching the highest-frequency option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by stress, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score ≥14 indicates probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> per EPDS guidelines. Patient reports <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the time, marked <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>inappropriate guilt</sym> daily, <sym>anxiety</sym> very often with panic episodes, and <sym>insomnia</sym> most nights, meeting <med>DSM-5</med> threshold for moderate-severe episode. Quote: <quote>heavy cloud that just hangs over everything</quote>. No self-harm ideation (Q10=0). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within 1 week for full evaluation and treatment plan
2. Request referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for psychotherapy (CBT or IPT) and consider antidepressant discussion
3. Share results with supportive partner/family so they can help with baby care and appointments
4. Begin gentle daily routine: 15 min outdoor walk, balanced meals, accept help with household tasks
5. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or progressive muscle relaxation when panic sensations start
6. Plan sleep strategy-split night shifts with partner, limit monitor checking to scheduled times, keep phone out of bed
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress
8. If thoughts of self-harm develop, go to nearest emergency department or call emergency services
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Summary

Patient-reported symptoms (≥ 2 weeks):
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Marked loss of interest/pleasure in activities, including infant care  
- Excessive inappropriate guilt/self-blame; feels “doing everything wrong”  
- Near-daily anxiety, multiple nocturnal panic attacks, catastrophic worries about infant safety  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia tied to rumination  
- Sense of being overwhelmed, difficulty completing basic tasks, crying while caring for baby  

Pattern: Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive symptoms with comorbid anxiety; no current self-harm ideation (patient explicitly denied).  

Screening significance: Elevated risk for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset and possible comorbid Panic Disorder/Generalized Anxiety Disorder; recommend prompt comprehensive clinical evaluation and safety-planning follow-up.
